analysis.one_liner: Adds a 10% surtax on individual income above $2 million, or $1 million for single filers.
analysis.headline: A bill adding a 10% tax on individual income above $2 million was introduced in April 2026 and has sat in the House Ways and Means Committee without a hearing or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would create a new 10% tax, on top of existing income tax, on each dollar of a person's income above $2 million a year — or above $1 million for people who file taxes singly. It applies to income from any source, including investments, and would start with the 2027 tax year. The bill was introduced on April 15, 2026 and sent to the House Ways and Means Committee, which handles tax bills; no hearing, committee vote, or floor vote has taken place.
analysis.who_benefits: If it passed, the direct benefit would be fiscal: the federal government would collect roughly 10 cents more on every dollar of income above the $2 million/$1 million thresholds, money that could reduce deficits or fund programs — though this bill itself does not earmark the revenue for anything. Households below the thresholds — the overwhelming majority of Americans — would pay nothing new under it. The bill's practical purpose is to shift more of the tax burden onto very high incomes, whatever Congress later does with the money.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Everyone except million-dollar earners, if revenue is used for them

how_it_helps.text: It adds a 10% tax on the portion of a person's income above $2 million ($1 million for single filers), raising revenue from a group that currently pays at ordinary rates on that income like everyone else.
The tax applies to income from any source — wages, investments, and pass-through business income — so high earners cannot escape it by recharacterizing earnings.
It takes effect for tax years beginning after December 31, 2026, so it would apply starting with the 2027 tax year if enacted.

analysis.who_pays: A small group of households with adjusted gross income above $2 million ($1 million for single filers) would pay the added 10% on the excess. The bill text also preserves the investment-interest deduction in calculating the surtax base, so investors who borrow to invest get to deduct that interest before the surtax applies — a break skewed toward leveraged investors. Because the bill does not specify a use for the revenue, there is no guaranteed offsetting benefit to anyone.
analysis.who_pays_short: Households earning over $2 million a year

drawbacks.text: The surtax base is 'modified adjusted gross income,' which subtracts investment-interest deductions from income. That carve-out lets investors who borrow to invest shrink the amount the surtax applies to, a break not available to wage earners.

The bill does not say what the revenue would be used for. It raises money for the Treasury generally; unless Congress later directs it to specific benefits or deficit reduction, ordinary people see no direct gain.
The $2 million joint / $1 million single thresholds are not indexed for inflation in the bill text, so over time the tax could reach people whose incomes only nominally crossed the line.
The surtax is imposed on top of existing taxes, adding a second layer of calculation on very high incomes; critics of surtaxes argue this complicates the code, though the affected group is small.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit — a meaningful tax increase on a very small group with very high incomes — is real but contingent: the bill never says what the money would fund, so its value to ordinary people depends entirely on how Congress spends it later. The costs are design flaws an honest supporter would acknowledge: the investment-interest carve-out lets the most leveraged investors shrink the base, the thresholds are not indexed for inflation, and the surtax does not address the main ways high earners defer or avoid tax ( unrealized gains, pass-through income). And the biggest caveat is political: with 10 supporters in a chamber run by the other party, the bill has essentially no path forward, so its benefits remain hypothetical.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the tax-writing committee the day it was introduced, and no hearing, markup, or floor vote has been scheduled since.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on April 15, 2026 and referred the same day to the House Committee on Ways and Means, the committee that handles tax legislation.
The action history shows no further steps: no hearing, no committee vote, and no floor action.
As of the latest record, the bill has one sponsor and 9 cosponsors, all Democrats, in a House where Republicans hold 223 of 441 seats.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one has had to act: households earning over $2 million keep their current tax treatment, and the bill's supporters have not yet forced the committee to take a position. Nothing is final — the Congress runs through January 2027.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: High earners, so far, keep the status quo

for.name: 9 of 217 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including Reps. Cohen, Deluzio, Norton, Tlaib, and Davis of Illinois as original cosponsors.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee (Chair Jason Smith, R-MO)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on April 15, 2026; the action record shows no hearing, markup, or vote scheduled since.

sides.party_line_note: All 10 supporters are Democrats (the sponsor plus 9 Democratic cosponsors); no Republican has signed on, and the Republican-controlled committee has taken no action.

industries.industry: Households with income above $2 million ($1 million single)
industries.note: These households would pay an added 10% on income above the threshold, on top of existing income tax. That is who the bill is written to tax, and it is who pays if it passes.

industries.industry: Highly leveraged investors (private equity, hedge funds, real estate)
industries.note: The bill's income definition subtracts investment-interest deductions, so investors who borrow to finance investments pay the surtax on a smaller base than pure wage earners at the same income. The carve-out softens the hit while keeping a tax break that ordinary wage earners cannot use.

analysis.trajectory: With a Republican majority and no recorded support from either party's leadership, the bill's likely path is the most common one for a minority-party tax bill: it stays in committee without a hearing or vote and expires when this Congress ends on January 3, 2027, unless supporters find a way to attach it to larger legislation, which a stand-alone surtax rarely achieves.
